groups.text: Here is a payment class with six fields, in Java and in Kotlin.
How many bytes does one Payment take?
JOL, OpenJDK's object layout tool, prints the real answer on J D K twenty-one: forty bytes, for both.
Every object starts with a header.
The mark word is eight bytes.
It holds the identity hash code, the G C age, and the lock bits that synchronized uses.
Then a class pointer, compressed to four bytes, says which class this is.
That's a twelve-byte header.
The fields come next, but not in the order you wrote them.
The long can't start at twelve, because a long must start at a multiple of eight.
So it goes to sixteen, and the J V M puts the int in the gap at twelve.
The boolean and the byte take one byte each.
After a two-byte gap come the references, four bytes each.
That's thirty-six bytes.
Objects start at multiples of eight, so the size rounds up to forty.
The rule: header, plus the fields, rounded up to eight.
twelve plus twenty-two is thirty-four, which rounds up to forty.
A reference on a sixty-four-bit machine should take eight bytes.
Here each one takes four, thanks to compressed oops: an oop is an ordinary object pointer.
Every object starts at a multiple of eight, so the last three bits of its address are always zero.
So the J V M drops them.
It stores a thirty-two-bit number, and shifts it left by three bits when it follows the reference.
two to the thirty-two slots, times eight bytes, is thirty-two GB.
Give the J V M a heap of thirty-two GB or more, and it turns compressed oops off.
References grow to eight bytes, and Payment to forty-eight.
An ArrayList of one thousand Integers grows by twenty-four percent.
